chapter: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
title: Lovett on Charlie Parker in Kansas City
summary: Lovett lived near Parker, says he was too far ahead for local players who would not let him sit in, and walked alone with his horn without a case.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Crook Goodwin and Art Smith here at the Afterhours in Kansas City. The end of Side One of this Tape Three we were discussing Lester Young and I referred briefly to Charlie Parker. I think now I'd like to go back to Charlie Parker and get your opinion, Baby, and later yours, Crook, on Charlie Parker and the whole Charlie Parker almost-mythology that's grown up about him. Baby, what do you know about Charlie Parker? When did you meet him, what did you think of him, how well did you know him?

I knew him pretty well. He lived a couple of blocks from me on 16th Street, Kansas City, Missouri, and when he first left here and went to New York, he was so far ahead of the alto players playing then that the guys laughed at him for playing so much out that they didn't know anything about and that goes for Johnny Hodges and all the guys.

They would sit around and listen to him and didn't want him to know they were out there. He was playing so much stuff that they couldn't play it, you understand what I mean, and that's where he made his fame in New York there. They finally got used to his playing, man, and everybody tried to play like Charlie Parker, which you know that.
Well, what did you know about him here in Kansas City? I mean, did you go and hear him, did you ever play with him?
Yes, I played with him a couple of

times I imagine and he -- Charlie was a guy, he would carry his horn, you know, up under his arm all the time and never had a case, you understand what I mean. He would pass my house every day, just walking.
Bent over with the horn?, in his arms, without a case.
Yeah, and he was so far ahead of the cats here, we wouldn't let him sit in at all.
They wouldn't let him sit in. Why not?
He was so far -- we didn't know what he was doing, what he was playing.
Well, there's a difference of opinion on that but you think because he was so far ahead of the guys like B.C. Canard and other great alto players around?
That's right.
That's what you're saying?
Yeah, and they would laugh at him, wouldn't let him sit in.
What kind of a life did he live here? Did he live by himself?
Always by himself. I never seen Charlie Parker --
Well, he had a family here, his mother and father. At least a mother...
Oh, the family was right down the street from me.
Oh, he lived with his mother?
Yeah, it was about a block and a half, 16th Street. Yeah, but Charlie never run with anybody. I never seen him with anybody, always by himself, walking with his head down.
I guess he was pretty young in those days. He was only about 35 when he died.
Yeah, he was a young guy. The guys wouldn't let him sit in. He was too far.
He was too good for them, is that what you're saying?
Yeah, they didn't know what he was playing, you understand what I mean? He went to New York and tore it up.
